claim: Queens of social insects have long lifespans.
source: The phenomenon that social insect queens live exceptionally long compared to solitary insects is widely recognized (Keller and Genoud, 1997; Carey, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keller and Genoud, 1997 and Carey, 2001

claim: Reproductive senescence seems to be negligible in social insect queens.
source: Strikingly, queens of social insects have long lifespans and reproductive senescence seems to be negligible.
evidence: Statement made in the abstract based on the study's findings

claim: Cardiocondyla obscurior queens shift to the production of sexuals in late life regardless of their absolute lifespan or the number of workers present.
source: By lifelong tracking of 99 Cardiocondyla obscurior (Formicidae: Myrmicinae) ant colonies, we find that queens shift to the production of sexuals in late life regardless of their absolute lifespan or the number of workers present.
evidence: Based on experimental data from tracking 99 colonies

claim: RNAseq analyses of old queens past their peak of reproductive performance showed the development of massive pathology while queens were still fertile.
source: Furthermore, RNAseq analyses of old queens past their peak of reproductive performance showed the development of massive pathology while queens were still fertile, leading to rapid death.
evidence: Based on RNAseq data comparing middle-aged and prope mortem queens

claim: The evolution of superorganismality is accompanied by 'continuusparity,' a life history strategy that combines continuous reproduction with a fitness peak late in life.
source: We conclude that the evolution of superorganismality is accompanied by 'continuusparity,' a life history strategy that is distinct from other iteroparous and semelparous strategies across the tree of life, in that it combines continuous reproduction with a fitness peak late in life.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings

claim: The selection shadow begins with maturity in iteroparous species.
source: This is known as the selection shadow, which begins with maturity (Williams, 1957) and may negatively affect reproductive performance and survival (i.e., senescence).
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams, 1957

claim: The treatment (varying worker number) did not affect total production of eggs.
source: The treatment (varying worker number) did not affect total production of eggs (package 'generalized linear mixed models using template finder' v. 1.1.2.3 in R) (Figure 1A, 10 vs. 20 workers: glmmTMB z-value = –0.38, p=0.70 and 10 vs. 30: z-value = –0.96, p=0.34)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The treatment did not affect worker pupae production.
source: or worker pupae (Figure 1B, 10 vs. 20 workers: glmmTMB z-value = 0.09, p=0.93 and 10 vs. 30: z-value = –0.39, p=0.70).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The treatment did not affect the lifespan of queens.
source: The treatment also did not affect the lifespan of queens (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A, Cox proportional hazard regression model, likelihood ratio test, X2 = 1.57, p=0.46)
evidence: Statistical analysis of survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A

claim: Queen lifespan was highly variable across treatments with a variation coefficient of 32.2%.
source: which was highly variable across treatments (variation coefficient: 32.2%, Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: Calculated variation coefficient from experimental data

claim: Queens with 10 workers produced significantly fewer queen pupae than queens with 20 workers.
source: Indeed, queens with 10 workers (n = 31) produced significantly fewer queen pupae than queens with 20 (n = 34) (glmmTMB z-value = 2.81, effect size=1.97, p=0.005)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Queens with 10 workers produced significantly fewer queen pupae than queens with 30 workers.
source: and 30 workers (n = 34) (glmmTMB z-value = 2.58, effect size=1.78, p=0.009, Figure 1C)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: There were no significant differences in queen pupae production between colonies with 20 and 30 workers.
source: with no significant differences between 20 and 30 workers (glmmTMB z-value = –0.49, p=0.877).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The median sex ratio (queen/queen + male pupae) across treatments was 0.85.
source: The median sex ratio (queen/queen + male pupae) across treatments was 0.85 (25 and 75% quantiles = 0.79 and 0.90)
evidence: Calculated from experimental data

claim: Total production of male pupae was unaffected by the treatment.
source: and total production of male pupae (two types of males occur in C. obscurior: winged and wingless) was unaffected by the treatment (10 vs. 20: glmmTMB z-value = 1.94, p=0.05 and 10 vs. 30: glmmTMB z-value = 1.52, p=0.13, Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claim: Queens produced very low numbers of winged males during their lifetime (mean = 0.36, median = 0).
source: Queens produced very low numbers of winged males during their lifetime (mean = 0.36, median = 0, N = 99).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data across 99 colonies

claim: A first peak in the investment in queen pupae occurred around 15 weeks after the colonies were established.
source: A first peak in the investment in queen pupae occurred around 15 weeks after the colonies were established (Figure 2A)
evidence: Observed in Figure 2A from experimental data

claim: Investment in queen pupae showed an increasing queen bias with age.
source: followed by an increasing queen bias with age (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed in Figure 2B from experimental data

claim: Pupa production is at its highest just before death.
source: In contrast, pupa production is at its highest just before death (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 from experimental data

claim: The caste ratio shift appeared to be a fixed trait, independent of colony size and queen lifespan.
source: Importantly, in C. obscurior this caste ratio shift appeared to be a fixed trait, independent of colony size and queen lifespan.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing consistent pattern across conditions

claim: Both queens with short and long lifespans exhibited late-life investment into queens.
source: Both queens with short and long lifespans (below and above the mean lifespan of 25 weeks, Figure 2C and D, respectively), equivalent to queens with low and high productivity, exhibited late-life investment into queens.
evidence: Observed in Figures 2C and 2D from experimental data

claim: Head width of workers was 2% significantly smaller in colonies with 10 workers than in colonies with 20 workers.
source: Head width of workers was 2% and 3% significantly smaller in colonies with 10 workers than in colonies with 20 (glmmTMB z-value = 2.22, p=0.026)
evidence: Statistical analysis of morphometric data shown in Figure 3

claim: Head width of workers was 3% significantly smaller in colonies with 10 workers than in colonies with 30 workers.
source: and 30 workers, respectively (glmmTMB z-value = 2.68, p=0.007, Figure 3)
evidence: Statistical analysis of morphometric data shown in Figure 3

claim: Head width of workers was not different between colonies with 20 and 30 workers.
source: but not different between colonies with 20 and 30 workers (glmmTMB z-value = 0.22, p=0.97).
evidence: Statistical analysis of morphometric data

claim: Relative fecundity reached its maximum after ~16 weeks, before completion of the median lifespan (~25 weeks), and then decreased.
source: After mean-standardizing queen age-specific mortality and fecundity (following Jones et al., 2014), we found that relative fecundity reached its maximum after ~16 weeks, before completion of the median lifespan (~25 weeks), and then decreased (Figure 4).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4 using mean-standardization method from Jones et al., 2014

claim: Relative investment in queen and male pupae reached its maximum late in life (~28 weeks).
source: Importantly, relative investment in queen and male pupae reached its maximum late in life (~28 weeks).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: C. obscurior ant queens exhibited a below-average level of adult mortality until week 30, after which mortality increased above the average level.
source: Furthermore, C. obscurior ant queens exhibited a below-average level of adult mortality until week 30, after which mortality increased above the average level (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Monitored workers in colonies with 10 or 20 nestmates did not differ in survival.
source: Monitored workers in colonies with 10 or 20 nestmates did not differ in survival (Cox proportional hazard regression model, likelihood ratio test, X2 = 0.06, p=0.8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of worker survival data

claim: The shape of mean-standardized mortality of workers was similar to that of queens.
source: Note that regardless of the differences in timescale, the shape of mean-standardized mortality of workers was similar to that of queens (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of mortality patterns shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Aging is a genetically fixed trait expressed by queens and workers alike.
source: This suggests that aging is a genetically fixed trait expressed by queens and workers alike.
evidence: Inference from the similar mortality patterns between queens and workers

claim: Of the 20,006 expressed genes in head-thorax tissue, 3565 (17.8%) genes were differentially expressed between middle-aged and prope mortem queens.
source: Of the 20,006 expressed genes in head-thorax tissue, 3565 (17.8%) genes were differentially expressed between middle-aged and prope mortem queens (after false discovery rate [FDR] adjustment p<0.001, DESeq2, Source data 9).
evidence: RNAseq analysis using DESeq2

claim: Of the differentially expressed genes in head-thorax tissue, 1725 genes (48%) were upregulated and 1840 genes (52%) were downregulated in prope mortem queens compared to middle-aged ones.
source: Of these, 1725 genes (48%) were upregulated and 1840 genes (52%) were downregulated in prope mortem queens compared to middle-aged ones.
evidence: RNAseq analysis results

claim: Gene Ontology term enrichment revealed signs of rapid physiological decay of prope mortem queens, such as reduced translation, proteasomal, ribosomal, and mitochondrial function.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) term enrichment revealed signs of rapid physiological decay of prope mortem queens, such as reduced translation, proteasomal, ribosomal, and mitochondrial function (Fisher test using the weight01 algorithm, p<0.05, Supplementary file 1B, Figure 5)
evidence: GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: Prope mortem queens showed increased splicing and transcript processing.
source: increased splicing, and transcript processing (Supplementary file 1C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Gene connectivity among gene expression networks was not affected by age in C. obscurior head-thorax tissue.
source: Another characteristic of aging, changes in gene connectivity among gene expression networks found in mice (Southworth et al., 2009), was not affected by age in C. obscurior (calculated using the softConnectivity and the biweight midcorrelation functions on gene networks for middle and prope mortem queens using WGCNA, and modeled using glmmTMB, z-value = −1.7, p=0.09).
evidence: WGCNA analysis of gene networks with citation to Southworth et al., 2009

claim: PCA ordination of the head-thorax tissue separated middle-aged and prope mortem queens by age but not by fertility.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) ordination of the head-thorax tissue separated middle-aged and prope mortem queens by age (PERMANOVA test, F-value = 7.59, p<0.001), but not by fertility (F-value = 1.09, p=0.26) or duplication percentage (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: PCA and PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: In the gaster tissue, 4832 (24.3%) of 19,925 expressed genes were differentially expressed between age groups.
source: In the gaster tissue, 4832 (24.3%) of 19,925 expressed genes were differentially expressed between age groups (after FDR adjustment p<0.001, DESeq2, Source data 10).
evidence: RNAseq analysis using DESeq2

claim: Of the differentially expressed genes in gaster tissue, 2306 genes were upregulated (48%) and 2526 downregulated (52%) in prope mortem queens compared to middle-aged queens.
source: Of these, 2306 genes were upregulated (48%) and 2526 downregulated (52%) in prope mortem queens compared to middle-aged queens.
evidence: RNAseq analysis results

claim: GO term enrichment showed that many fundamental processes were affected in prope mortem queens, such as DNA damage, telomere maintenance, and enrichment of transcription processes.
source: GO term enrichment likewise showed that many fundamental processes were affected in prope mortem queens, such as DNA damage, telomere maintenance, and enrichment of transcription processes (Supplementary file 1D, Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
evidence: GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4

claim: Gene connectivity among gene co-expression networks in the gaster was significantly different between prope mortem and middle-aged queens.
source: In contrast to head-thorax tissue, gene connectivity among gene co-expression networks in the gaster was significantly different (prope mortem queens: median = 69.45; middle-aged queens: median = 52.56) (glmmTMB, z-value = −19.5, p<2e-16)
evidence: WGCNA analysis of gene networks

claim: The PCA of the 500 most variable expressed genes in gaster tissue shows that the samples group according to age, fertility level, and the percentage of duplicated reads.
source: The PCA of the 500 most variable expressed genes in gaster tissue shows that the samples group according to age (PERMANOVA test, F-value = 13.91, p<0.001), fertility level (F-value = 1.95, p=0.04), and also the percentage of duplicated reads in the libraries (F-value = 4.83, p=0.002, Figure 5—figure supplement 6A and B).
evidence: PCA and PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6

claim: 104 GO terms were significantly enriched in both head-thorax and gaster tissues.
source: In spite of these discrepancies between tissue types, 104 GO terms were significantly enriched in both tissues, of these 44 in prope mortem queens (Supplementary file 1F) and 60 in middle-aged queens (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: GO term enrichment analysis comparing both tissues

claim: Signs of similar physiological pathologies occur in reproductive and non-reproductive tissue.
source: Thus, signs of similar physiological pathologies occur in reproductive and non-reproductive tissue.
evidence: Inference from the overlap of GO terms enriched in both tissues

claim: Most new queens were produced by queens older than the mean queen lifespan.
source: In C. obscurior, most new queens were produced by queens older than the mean queen lifespan, indicating that queens continue to experience strong selection at high ages.
evidence: Inference from the experimental data showing late-life investment in sexuals

claim: Relative mortality did not increase directly after maturity or after total egg production started decreasing, but after the production of sexual pupae had reached its maximum.
source: Strikingly, relative mortality did not increase directly after maturity or after total egg production started decreasing, but after the production of sexual pupae had reached its maximum.
evidence: Analysis of mortality and reproduction data from the experiment

claim: Transcriptome profiles of prope mortem queens shortly after the investment peak revealed signs of a broad range of physiological pathologies.
source: Accordingly, transcriptome profiles of prope mortem queens shortly after this investment peak, which produced decreasing numbers of eggs, revealed signs of a broad range of physiological pathologies.
evidence: RNAseq analysis of prope mortem queens

claim: The changes in gene expression seemed stronger in the gaster but to a similar extent occurred in head and thorax.
source: The changes seemed stronger in the gaster (e.g., percentage of duplicated reads), which contains the reproductive organs and most of the digestive system, but to a similar extent occurred in head and thorax, containing most neuronal and muscle tissue.
evidence: Comparison of RNAseq results between tissues

claim: A comparative transcriptomic study of 8-week young queens with fully mature C. obscurior queens at or close to their peak fecundity (18 weeks old) did not find signs indicative of aging.
source: Strikingly, a comparative transcriptomic study of 8-week young queens with fully mature C. obscurior queens at or close to their peak fecundity (18 weeks old) did not find signs indicative of aging, but in comparison to aged Drosophila flies an opposite regulation of processes (e.g., cellular ketone, carbohydrate, and organic acid metabolic processes) and genes (e.g., ref(2)P, emp, P5cr-2, CCHa2, NLaz, Sirt6) involved in aging (von Wyschetzki et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to von Wyschetzki et al., 2015 study

claim: A gene co-expression network study showed higher connectivity in middle-aged queens, indicating increased transcriptional regulation with age.
source: Furthermore, a gene co-expression network study using the same data showed higher connectivity in middle-aged queens, indicating increased transcriptional regulation with age (Harrison et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to Harrison et al., 2021 study

claim: The physiology of queens is maintained until the fitness peak is reached, at which time they undergo physiological deterioration, while still being reproductively active.
source: Together, this suggests that the physiology of queens is maintained until the fitness peak is reached, at which time they undergo physiological deterioration, while still being reproductively active.
evidence: Inference from the combined transcriptomic and reproductive data

claim: Continuusparity is the combination of lifelong continuous reproduction and increasing fitness returns late in life.
source: We propose that the evolution of 'continuusparity' (Lat.: 'continuus' meaning incessant/successive; and 'parere' meaning giving birth), that is, the combination of lifelong continuous reproduction and increasing fitness returns late in life, underlies the delay of the selection shadow, the maintenance of selection strength against age-specific mortality, a brief phase of senescence late in life, and finally reproductive death.
evidence: Theoretical framework proposed by the authors based on their findings

claim: Continuusparity emerges as a combination of iteroparous and semelparous characteristics.
source: 'Continuusparity' emerges as a combination of iteroparous and semelparous characteristics: reproduction resembling continuous iteroparous species but without the inter-parous nonreproductive breaks, during which nests are built, mating occurs, resources are acquired, etc.
evidence: Theoretical framework proposed by the authors

claim: The iteroparous solitary ancestor of ants is thought to be related to mud dauber wasps (Sphecidae) and cockroach wasps (Ampulicidae).
source: The iteroparous solitary ancestor of ants is thought to be related to mud dauber wasps (Sphecidae) and cockroach wasps (Ampulicidae) (Ward, 2014), parasitoid wasps with mass provisioning.
evidence: Citation to Ward, 2014

claim: Continuous reproduction is possible because no extra time or energy is necessary for further acquisition of resources, brood care, territoriality, etc., because of the extended phenotype, the colony.
source: Continuous reproduction is possible because no extra time or energy is necessary for further acquisition of resources, brood care, territoriality, etc., because of the extended phenotype, the colony.
evidence: Theoretical explanation based on superorganism concept

claim: Continuusparity and its effect on the shape of queen aging is a property of superorganismality.
source: We propose that continuusparity and its effect on the shape of queen aging is a property of superorganismality, and that this life history strategy ultimately underlies the evolution of long lifespans in social insects.
evidence: Theoretical framework proposed by the authors

claim: There are no genes/pathways with antagonistic pleiotropic effects in social insect queens because there is no 'later in life' past the fitness peak.
source: With respect to which proximate mechanisms regulate aging in social insects, this framework predicts that there are no genes/pathways with antagonistic pleiotropic effects because there is no 'later in life' past the fitness peak.
evidence: Theoretical prediction based on the continuusparity framework

claim: C. obscurior is probably the best studied ant species with respect to aging due to the relatively short lifespan of queens (~6 months).
source: C. obscurior is probably the best studied ant species with respect to aging due to the relatively short lifespan of queens (~6 months).
evidence: Statement about the species' suitability for aging research

claim: C. obscurior colonies comprise a few queens (body length ~3 mm), a few dozen workers (~2 mm), and nest in small cavities in dead twigs, aborted fruits, rolled leaves, under bark, etc., in trees and shrubs.
source: Colonies comprise a few queens (body length ~3 mm), a few dozen workers (~2 mm), and nest in small cavities in dead twigs, aborted fruits, rolled leaves, under bark, etc., in trees and shrubs (Schrader et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to Schrader et al., 2014

claim: Virgin C. obscurior queens usually mate once with related wingless males inside the natal colony.
source: Virgin queens usually mate once with related wingless males inside the natal colony (Heinze and Hölldobler, 1993; Schmidt et al., 2016; Heinze and Hölldobler, 2019)
evidence: Citations to Heinze and Hölldobler, 1993; Schmidt et al., 2016; Heinze and Hölldobler, 2019

claim: New C. obscurior colonies are formed by budding of colony fragments.
source: generally stay in the nest, and new colonies are formed by budding of colony fragments.
evidence: Description of the species' reproductive mode

claim: Queens that lay more eggs (total output and weekly rate) live longer than less fecund queens, irrespective of body size.
source: Queens that lay more eggs (total output and weekly rate) live longer than less fecund queens, irrespective of body size (Kramer et al., 2015)
evidence: Citation to Kramer et al., 2015

claim: C. obscurior queens seem to evade the common trade-off between reproduction and maintenance.
source: and thus seem to evade the common trade-off between reproduction and maintenance.
evidence: Inference from the positive relationship between fecundity and lifespan

claim: 138 freshly eclosed queens from stock colonies of a Japanese population were set up for the experiment.
source: We set up 138 freshly eclosed queens from stock colonies of a Japanese population (OypB, from the Oonoyama Park in Naha, Okinawa) established in the laboratory since 2011.
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: The experiment took place between January 2019 and January 2020.
source: The experiment took place between January 2019 and January 2020.
evidence: Description of experimental timeline

claim: Queens were allowed to mate with a single wingless male and were placed in nest boxes with either 10, 20, or 30 workers from the maternal colony.
source: Queens were allowed to mate with a single wingless male and were placed in nest boxes with either 10, 20, or 30 workers from the maternal colony to establish monogynous colonies, for lifetime production and RNAseq (n = 46 each).
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: The numbers of workers (10, 20, 30) represent the naturally occurring number in the field and correspond to the first, median, and third quantile of number of workers in this population.
source: These numbers of workers represent the naturally occurring number in the field and correspond to the first, median, and third quantile of number of workers in this population (n = 62, median = 28.5, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Field data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: C. obscurior workers are sterile, and all produced offspring originated from the focal queen.
source: C. obscurior workers are sterile, and all produced offspring originated from the focal queen.
evidence: Statement about the species' biology

claim: The number of counted eggs correlates with the production of workers, queens, and the workers and queens together.
source: The number of counted eggs correlates with the production of workers, queens, and the workers and queens together (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C, Kendall's rank correlation test, p<0.001: eggs-worker pupae, τ = 0.70; eggs-queen pupae, τ = 0.59; eggs-worker and queen pupae, τ = 0.73).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: 40 focal unmarked worker pupae were set up in individual colonies with 10 or 20 marked workers to examine worker aging.
source: To examine worker aging, 40 focal unmarked worker pupae were set up in individual colonies with 10 or 20 marked workers (n = 20 each).
evidence: Description of experimental setup for worker aging study

claim: 360 freshly eclosed adult workers were sampled monthly for head width measurements from the third to sixth month of the queen's life.
source: 360 freshly eclosed adult workers were sampled monthly for head width measurements (from the third to sixth month of the queen's life, and up to five workers depending on availability).
evidence: Description of morphometric sampling

claim: A Gompertz model was selected as best-fitted model for mortality based on the deviance information criterion (DIC) values.
source: A Gompertz model was selected as best-fitted model based on the deviance information criterion (DIC) values, over the logistic and Weibull models (Supplementary file 1H) using the R package BaSTA (Survival Bayesian Trajectory Analysis, v. 1.9.5).
evidence: Model selection analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: 18 queens at age 19–21 weeks were sacrificed for RNAseq based on egg productivity until week 18.
source: To obtain samples of low, medium, and highly productive queens, 18 queens at age 19–21 weeks were sacrificed for RNAseq based on egg productivity until week 18.
evidence: Description of experimental design for RNAseq

claim: An additional 18 queens were monitored until they showed decreasing fertility and signs of senescence, then sacrificed (28–49 weeks old).
source: An additional 18 queens were monitored until they showed decreasing fertility (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and one or more of the following signs of senescence: lethargy, loss of mobility, presence outside the nest, and/or harassment by workers. These senescent queens were also selected based on low, medium, and high fertility, and then sacrificed (28–49 weeks old).
evidence: Description of experimental design for RNAseq

claim: Total RNA was extracted using the ReliaPrep kit (Promega) from the 72 samples (36 queens, two samples per queen: head-thorax and gaster).
source: Total RNA was extracted using the ReliaPrep kit (Promega) from the 72 samples (36 queens, two samples per queen: head-thorax and gaster).
evidence: Description of RNA extraction method

claim: Spike-In RNA Variant Controls (SIRV-Set 3 Lexogen) were spiked to a 2% fraction of the total RNA.
source: Spike-In RNA Variant Controls (SIRV-Set 3 Lexogen #05101‚ Lot 5746/001492) were spiked to a 2% fraction of the total RNA (measured using Bioanalyzer – Agilent Technologies).
evidence: Description of RNA quality control method

claim: 8 of the 72 samples showed RIN values below 7 (gaster samples from older queens that seemed more degraded).
source: 8 of the 72 samples showed RIN values below 7 (gaster samples from older queens that seemed more degraded).
evidence: RNA quality assessment results
